\section[quaesō]{quaesō — please (I ask)}

\label{lesson:LA-C03-quaeso}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Latin has no word that simply means "please." Instead you say what you're actually doing: \textbf{asking.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{quaesō} — said \emph{KWAI-so} (qu = \textbf{kw}, ae = \textbf{eye}) — literally means \textbf{"I ask"} or \textbf{"I beg."} Romans dropped it into a sentence exactly where English drops \emph{please}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Dā mihi aquam, \textbf{quaesō}} — "Give me water, \textbf{please}" (lit. "…I ask").
\end{quote}

It's a worn-down cousin of the verb \textbf{quaerere}, "to seek, to ask" — the same root English took for \textbf{query}, \textbf{quest}, \textbf{question}, \textbf{require} and \textbf{inquire}. So \emph{quaesō} is, at heart, "I'm seeking {[}this{]} of you."
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Because there's no single word, Latin had a small kit of polite moves — worth meeting so the absence doesn't feel like a gap:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{sīs} — a squeezed \textbf{sī vīs}, "\textbf{if you wish}" (to one person); plural \textbf{sultis} (\emph{sī vultis}). This is the \emph{same} "if you wish" strategy French will use in \emph{s'il te plaît}.
  \item \textbf{amābō tē} — literally "\textbf{I will love you}" — a warm, coaxing "please," the way English might say "be a dear."
\end{itemize}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "quaesō" — \emph{KWAI-so}, "I ask"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: in place — "Dā mihi aquam, quaesō"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the "if you wish" version — "sīs" (from \emph{sī vīs}){]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What did Romans literally say instead of "please"? (\textbf{quaesō} — "I ask/beg.") What verb is it from, and which English words share that root? (\textbf{quaerere} "to seek" — \emph{query, quest, require}.) What does \textbf{sīs} stand for? (\emph{\textbf{sī vīs}}, "if you wish" — the same idea French uses in \emph{s'il te plaît}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
